metadata.title: Analysis of PISA 2006 Preferred Items Ranking Using the Percent-Correct Method (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses PISA 2006 item-level percent-correct statistics computed as weighted proportions of observed scores over maximum possible scores, where the denominator and numerator are summed across students who responded to each item and are weighted with PISA student weights. The analysis is conducted at the country level by averaging item percent-correct values over subsets of science items that each country rated as highest priority for inclusion. The manuscript does not report the specific weight variable name or whether replicate weights were used, and it does not re-estimate proficiency scales using the full PISA item response model. Because the study is an approximate percent-correct ranking exercise rather than a PV-based achievement re-scaling, the weighting role is limited to computing item percent-correct inputs, not to fitting an ML model.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not estimate or analyze cognitive achievement scores via PISA plausible values; instead, it computes an approximate percent-correct statistic at the item level and then ranks countries using averages over item subsets. Missing-data handling is therefore not described in terms of PV imputation/deletion, because the dependent quantities are item percent-correct proportions derived from students who responded to each item. This omission is a reporting gap for missingness at the student/item level, but it is not central to PV-based missingness procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA 2006 science items and the country-provided priority-for-inclusion ratings (5-point scale) for Field Trial items. Two ranking sets are produced: (1) using only new PISA 2006 items rated at the highest priority level (5), excluding countries that rated fewer than five items at level 5 (e.g., Spain and Switzerland are excluded in this subset because they rated only two items at level 5); and (2) using a larger item pool that includes 22 science items from previous PISA cycles (used for score linking) plus each country’s highly preferred items for PISA 2006, which increases stability. For countries that rated no items at level 5 (e.g., Macao-China, Montenegro, Slovak Republic), the highest rated level (4) is used as the preferred set. Countries that did not provide item ratings or rated all items at the highest level are excluded from the preferred-item ranking basis as described in the appendix (Table A1).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper analyzes how stable PISA 2006 country rankings are when the ranking is recomputed using an approximate “average percent-correct” method rather than the full PISA scaling model. Each country’s experts rated science Field Trial items for priority of inclusion on a five-point scale; the study then forms multiple item subsets corresponding to each country’s preferred items and computes item percent-correct (weighted by PISA student weights) and country average percent-correct across those subsets. Rankings are compared across (i) all PISA 2006 science items, (ii) only new PISA 2006 items, and (iii) preferred-item subsets with and without the 22 score-linking items from previous cycles. The paper finds remarkable consistency with the OECD (2007) initial PISA 2006 ranking, with only a few countries showing systematic rank shifts that are small and comparable to sampling error, suggesting that PISA rankings are robust to reasonable differences in item preference. It also concludes that experts cannot reliably predict which items would advantage their country’s final ranking, and that robustness depends on having a sufficiently large item pool that accommodates diverse preferences.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a methodological/assessment-design analysis rather than an empirical ML prediction study: it recomputes rankings using an approximate percent-correct approach and compares them to the official PISA 2006 ranking. As a result, there is no ML model training, no PV-based dependent variable, and no reported ML performance metrics. The paper also does not provide a student-level analytic sample size or per-country student counts, because the unit of analysis is the country ranking derived from item-level percent-correct statistics.
